summary.text: A redshift is an increase in the wavelength, or a decrease in the frequency, of electromagnetic radiation such as light.
Astronomy has three forms: Doppler redshifts from relative motion, gravitational redshift from radiation escaping gravity, and cosmological redshifts from the universe expanding.
It is written as z, the fractional change in wavelength, and automated redshift surveys help map the large-scale structure of the universe.

paragraphs.heading: Stretched light
paragraphs.text: A redshift is a lengthening of the wavelength of electromagnetic radiation, such as light, which is the same thing as a drop in its frequency. The reverse change, a shorter wavelength with higher frequency and energy, is called a blueshift. Astronomers write the size of a redshift as z, the fractional change in wavelength, which is positive for a redshift and negative for a blueshift.

paragraphs.heading: Three causes
paragraphs.text: In astronomy and cosmology, redshift comes in three forms. A Doppler redshift comes from the source and the observer moving relative to each other. A gravitational redshift happens as radiation climbs out of a gravitational potential. A cosmological redshift comes from the expansion of the universe itself. Other processes, such as scattering and optical effects, can also shift frequency, but those changes can be told apart and are not usually called redshift.

paragraphs.heading: What it shows us
paragraphs.text: Automated surveys of redshifts are an important way to learn about the structure of the universe on the largest scales. Strong redshifts can make a gamma ray look like an X-ray, or turn visible light into radio waves. The radiation from the Big Bang, once at 3000 kelvin, has been shifted all the way down to become the 3 K cosmic microwave background. Smaller shifts appear when astronomers spread out the light of objects in space, and the same effect is put to work on Earth in Doppler radar and radar guns.

paragraphs.heading: From sound to starlight
paragraphs.text: The effect is named after Christian Doppler, an Austrian mathematician who gave the first known physical explanation of it in 1842. In 1845, the Dutch scientist Christophorus Buys Ballot tested the idea with sound and confirmed it. Doppler rightly predicted that it would hold for every kind of wave, and he suggested that the varied colors of stars might come from their motion relative to Earth. By 1868, William Huggins was the first to work out the speed of a star moving away from Earth by studying shifts in its spectrum.

paragraphs.heading: Redshift and the expanding universe
paragraphs.text: Starting in 1912, Vesto Slipher found that the Andromeda Galaxy was blueshifted, meaning it was moving toward Earth. Until 1923 nobody was sure what the nebulae were, but by that year Edwin Hubble had shown they were galaxies and devised a way to measure their distance using Cepheid variable stars. In 1929 he combined those distances with redshifts from Slipher and Milton Humason and reported a rough link between redshift and distance, now called Hubble's law. By early 1930, these measurements and new theoretical models together showed that the universe had a history and that its expansion could be studied with physics and observation.

paragraphs.heading: Wrong turns along the way
paragraphs.text: When cosmological redshifts were first found, Fritz Zwicky proposed an alternative called tired light. Observations of time stretching in type Ia supernovae have since largely ruled it out. In the 1960s, quasars looked like very blue points of light and were first taken for unusual stars, which led some to suggest they were nearer than their redshifts implied. A burst of theory and observation then showed they were very powerful objects at great distances.
